section.title: The Annunciation and the Magnificat
section.sectionRationale: The angel who visited the temple now comes to a village girl. Gabriel tells Mary she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear the Son of the Most High, who will reign on David's throne forever. Mary, unlike Zechariah, answers in trust: I am the Lord's servant. She hurries to Elizabeth, whose unborn child leaps for joy, and there she pours out the Magnificat, a song of a God who lifts the lowly and fills the hungry. It is one movement, from the announcement of the incarnation to the praise it draws forth.
section.thesis: God stoops to a lowly virgin to give the world its King, and the humble faith of Mary answers with a song that magnifies the God who scatters the proud, lifts up the lowly, and keeps His promise to Abraham forever.
section.frameNote: Six beats: Gabriel comes to Mary; the promise of Jesus, Son of the Most High; the Holy Spirit and Mary's yes; Mary visits Elizabeth; the Magnificat; and Mary's return home.

units.label: Gabriel comes to Mary
units.note: greetings, you who are highly favored

verses.text: In the sixth month, God sent the angel Gabriel to a town in Galilee called Nazareth,
to a virgin pledged in marriage to a man named Joseph, who was of the house of David. And the virgin’s name was Mary.
The angel appeared to her and said, “Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.”
Mary was greatly troubled at his words and wondered what kind of greeting this might be.

units.label: The promise of Jesus, Son of the Most High
units.note: the throne of His father David

verses.text: So the angel told her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found {{charis|favor}} with God.
Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus.
He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David,
and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!”

units.label: The Holy Spirit and Mary's yes

verses.text: “How can this be,” Mary asked the angel, “since I am a virgin?”
The angel replied, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God.
Look, even Elizabeth your relative has conceived a son in her old age, and she who was called barren is in her sixth month.
For no word from God will ever fail.”
“I am the Lord’s servant,” Mary answered. “May it happen to me according to your word.” Then the angel left her.
In those days Mary got ready and hurried to a town in the hill country of Judah,
where she entered the home of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.
When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
In a loud voice she exclaimed, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!
And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
For as soon as the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy.
Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.”
Then Mary said: “My soul {{megalyno|magnifies}} the Lord,
and my spirit rejoices in God my {{soter|Savior}}!
For He has looked with favor on the {{tapeinosis|humble state}} of His servant. From now on all generations will call me blessed.
For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name.
His {{eleos|mercy}} extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation.
He has performed mighty deeds with His arm; He has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts.
He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble.
He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty.
He has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful,
as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.”
Mary stayed with Elizabeth for about three months and then returned home.

charis.gloss: Grace, favor, undeserved kindness. Gabriel tells Mary she has found favor with God. This is not a reward for her merit but the free grace of God, who chooses the lowly and unlikely to accomplish His purpose.

megalyno.gloss: To magnify, enlarge, declare great. The Latin for this word, magnificat, gives Mary's song its name. To magnify the Lord is not to make Him bigger but to let one's whole life declare and enjoy His greatness.

soter.gloss: Savior, deliverer, rescuer. Mary rejoices in God her Savior, showing that she knows her own need of saving grace. The title runs through Luke, who loves to name Jesus as the Savior for all people.

tapeinosis.gloss: Low estate, humble condition, humiliation. God looks with favor on the low place of His servant, the very theme of the song: He lifts the lowly and casts down the proud, echoing Hannah's prayer.

eleos.gloss: Mercy, steadfast covenant love, the Greek that renders the Hebrew hesed. God's mercy reaches from generation to generation to those who fear Him, and in the incarnation He remembers to be merciful to Israel as He promised Abraham.

basic.context: Six months after Gabriel visited Zechariah, the same angel comes to Mary, a young virgin in Nazareth pledged to Joseph. He greets her as highly favored and tells her she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son, Jesus, the Son of the Most High, who will reign on David's throne forever. Mary asks how this can be, and when told it is the Spirit's work, she answers in faith: I am the Lord's servant. She hurries to her relative Elizabeth, whose unborn baby leaps for joy, and there Mary sings the Magnificat, praising the God who lifts up the lowly and keeps His promise to Israel.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the annunciation alongside the visit to Zechariah: both are angelic announcements, but Mary's trusting question and glad surrender stand in gentle contrast to the old priest's doubt. The Magnificat is soaked in the Old Testament, especially Hannah's song, so Mary sings not private feelings but the great biblical theme of God overturning the proud order of the world. The key questions are who this child is and what kind of God so exalts the lowly.
basic.originalLanguages: Mary has found charis, grace, with God. Her soul megalyno, magnifies, the Lord, from which the song takes its Latin name Magnificat. She rejoices in God her soter, her Savior, because He has looked on her tapeinosis, her low estate, and shows eleos, covenant mercy, from generation to generation.
basic.typology: Mary's song deliberately echoes Hannah's prayer, casting Mary as the true daughter of Israel's hope. The promise of an everlasting throne fulfills God's covenant with David, and the child conceived by the Spirit is the long-awaited seed of Abraham through whom all nations are blessed.
basic.christ: The child is named Jesus, the Son of the Most High and Son of God, conceived by the Holy Spirit. He is the promised King of David's line whose kingdom will never end. This is the heart of the passage: God Himself is coming into the world as a human child.
basic.god: God is the Mighty One who is also merciful, who chooses the lowly, scatters the proud, fills the hungry, and remembers His promises. He is Mary's Savior, and salvation is entirely His initiative and gift.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 2 gives Hannah's song, the pattern for the Magnificat. 2 Samuel 7 records the promise of an everlasting throne to David. Isaiah 7 foretells the virgin who bears Immanuel. And Genesis 12 records the promise to Abraham that Mary sees being kept.
basic.oneStory: The King promised to David and the seed promised to Abraham now begin to arrive, not through the mighty but through a humble girl who believes God. Mary's song announces the great reversal the gospel brings: the God who lifts the lowly is coming to save.

context.literary:
This section is the second panel of a pair, set beside the announcement to Zechariah in Luke 1:5-25 and tied to it by a time marker, 'in the sixth month,' verse 26. Each scene has the same bones: an angel appears, fear is met with 'Do not be afraid,' a son is promised and named, his future is described, an objection is raised, and a sign is given. The differences carry the meaning. Gabriel goes to the temple at Jerusalem for the priest and to an obscure Galilean town for the girl, the first son is 'great in the sight of the Lord,' 1:15, while the second will be 'called the Son of the Most High,' verse 32.

The section then divides into the annunciation, verses 26 to 38, and the visitation, verses 39 to 56. Mary's answer in verse 38 and her song in verses 46 to 55 frame her as a servant: she calls herself the Lord's servant in 38, and says God has looked on 'His servant' in 48. The word servant, doule, brackets the whole.

The Magnificat itself is a poem in three movements. Verses 46 to 50 are personal: my soul, my spirit, me, and the God who did great things for me. Verses 51 to 53 widen into the great reversals, in which the proud, the rulers and the rich are brought down and the humble and the hungry are lifted. Verses 54 and 55 close on Israel and the promise to Abraham. The movement is from Mary's own story to the world's, and from there to the covenant that holds both.

The poem is Hebrew in form. Its lines are balanced pairs, in which the second line restates or sharpens the first, as in 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble,' verse 52. Almost every phrase has an Old Testament source, so that the song reads like a weaving of Scripture, with Hannah's prayer, 1 Samuel 2:1-10, as the main thread. Luke gives Mary, a young girl from an unregarded town, the voice of the Psalms.
context.historical:
Nazareth was a small village in lower Galilee, never named in the Old Testament, and the reputation of the place was low, as Nathanael's question in John 1:46 shows. Mary was 'pledged in marriage,' verse 27, which in Jewish custom was a binding agreement, entered into by the families, more than a modern engagement. The couple were considered legally committed, though the wedding and the move into the husband's home came later, usually after about a year. A pregnancy in that interval was a scandal, which is why Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side, Matthew 1:18-25.

Joseph was 'of the house of David,' verse 27. By the first century this was an honourable but not an exalted claim. David's line had not sat on a throne for six hundred years, and Judea was ruled by Herod, an Edomite appointed by Rome. When Gabriel promises 'the throne of His father David,' verse 32, he is promising something that, in the political world of the day, looked impossible.

Mary's visit takes her south to 'a town in the hill country of Judah,' verse 39, a journey of several days. Elizabeth was her 'relative,' verse 36, and the ties between the two families may be through the priestly line. The trip took Mary from a Galilean village to the heart of Judah's religious world, and Luke tells us only that she 'got ready and hurried,' verse 39.

The Magnificat belongs to a tradition of Israelite piety that scholars often associate with the 'poor' or 'humble' of the land. Zephaniah promises that God will leave 'a meek and humble people' who trust in His name, Zephaniah 3:12. Such people were poor materially, often oppressed by their rulers, and held their hope in God alone. Mary's song speaks in their voice, and it was sung against a backdrop of heavy taxation, foreign troops, and a client king's building schemes. The reversals of verses 51 to 53 would have sounded, to those first hearers, like politics and prophecy at once.
context.canonical:
Gabriel's promise to Mary is built from the covenant with David. The LORD told David, 'I will raise up your descendant after you... and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever,' 2 Samuel 7:12-13, and 'your throne will be established forever,' 7:16. The psalmist repeated it, Psalm 132:11, and Isaiah gave it its fullest form: a child to be born, 'He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom,' Isaiah 9:6-7. Daniel adds the language of a kingdom 'that will never be destroyed,' Daniel 7:14, and Luke 1:33 echoes it: 'His kingdom will never end!'

The virgin conception stands against Isaiah 7:14, 'the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel,' which Matthew explicitly quotes, Matthew 1:22-23. The words of verse 35, 'the power of the Most High will overshadow you,' recall the cloud that covered the tent of meeting when the glory of the LORD filled it, Exodus 40:34-35, and the cloud on the mountain at the transfiguration, Luke 9:34. Verse 37, 'no word from God will ever fail,' draws on Genesis 18:14, the question put to Abraham.

The Magnificat reaches back to Hannah's song, 1 Samuel 2:1-10, which also praised a God who humbles the mighty and exalts the poor, and to the Psalms: Psalm 113:7-8 on raising the poor, Psalm 107:9 on filling the hungry, Psalm 98:3 on remembering His love to Israel, Psalm 103:17 on mercy from generation to generation.

The song is also taken up by what follows. The Beatitudes and woes of Luke 6:20-26 turn the song's reversal into the teaching of Jesus: 'Blessed are you who are poor' and 'Woe to you who are rich.' Jesus says that 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled,' Luke 14:11, and Paul says God 'chose the lowly and despised things of the world,' 1 Corinthians 1:28. Paul's summary of the person of Christ, 'descendant of David according to the flesh... declared with power to be the Son of God,' Romans 1:3-4, is the same pair of titles Gabriel gives.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants Theophilus, and every later reader, to know who Jesus is before the story of His life begins. Gabriel's words in verses 31 to 35 are the fullest identification of Jesus in the opening chapters: He is a human child with a human name, Jesus, a king in the line of David whose kingdom has no end, the Son of the Most High, the Holy One, and the Son of God. These are not titles given later by a church. They are announced from heaven before He is born.

Luke also wants us to see what kind of person God chooses. Mary is not a priest, not wealthy, not famous. She is from a village of no account and has no standing. Luke makes this the heart of the passage by having her say, 'He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant,' verse 48. The God who is about to do the greatest thing in history chooses a person whom the world would not notice, and Luke means for readers to take from that who God is and how He works.

He wants us to read Mary's answer as the model of faith, not of mere passivity. 'I am the Lord's servant. May it happen to me according to your word,' verse 38, is a free and costly yes. She knows what it may cost her reputation and her future, and she says it anyway. Elizabeth confirms the reading in verse 45: 'Blessed is she who has believed.'

Finally, Luke wants the Magnificat to set the keynote for his whole Gospel. The reversal it sings, of the humble lifted and the proud brought low, is what Jesus will teach and enact from Nazareth to the cross, and Luke says it first in the mouth of a girl who is carrying the one who will do it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The annunciation describes a unique event: a virgin conception that happens once. It is not a pattern for how God usually brings children into the world, and it is not repeated. What carries forward is not the miracle but the response. Mary's 'May it happen to me according to your word' is a model for believers who hear a word from God that is costly, but it is not a promise that obedience will be comfortable. She is told in the next chapter that a sword will pierce her own soul, Luke 2:35.

The song of Mary is a hymn of praise, not a program. It describes what God has done and will do, and the verbs are God's, not human beings'. It does not tell the poor to rise against the rich, or tell the rich to feel guilty about being rich. It does speak a warning to those who trust in their own power, and a promise to those who wait on God. Christians have often drawn from it a concern for the hungry and the lowly, and that is faithful so long as it is rooted in what God has done in Christ, and comes from the spirit of Luke 6:20-26 and James 4:6, 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.'

Mary is honoured by Scripture, and the angel and Elizabeth both bless her, verses 28 and 42. The passage invites us to honour her as the believing servant through whom the Saviour came. It never asks that she be worshipped or prayed to. She herself directs all praise to God, 'My soul magnifies the Lord,' verse 46, and says that she needs God as 'my Savior,' verse 47.

debates.question: What does Mary mean by 'since I am a virgin'?

views.label: She is describing her present state
views.case: The Greek is literally 'since I do not know a man.' Pledged to Joseph but not yet married, Mary is simply saying that she has had no relations. Her question is how a conception could happen before marriage, and Gabriel answers that it will be by the Holy Spirit, verse 35. Matthew 1:25 says Joseph 'had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son.' Most Protestant interpreters read it this way.

views.label: She had resolved to remain a virgin
views.case: Some in the church, beginning with the early centuries, read the question as a sign of a standing resolve of virginity. A woman about to marry would not ask how she could conceive unless she had decided not to. Augustine took this view, and it supports the tradition of Mary's perpetual virginity, held by the Catholic and Orthodox churches and by some of the Reformers.

views.label: The question is literary, not psychological
views.case: A third view treats the question as a device by which Luke can give Gabriel the chance to explain the conception. Whatever Mary's inner state, what matters is the answer, which settles that the child's origin is the Spirit's act, not a human father's.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle what Mary had resolved, and the whole weight of the passage lies on Gabriel's answer. What every view must hold is that Jesus' conception was the Spirit's work, and that Mary asked in faith and was neither rebuked nor doubted.

debates.question: What does it mean that Mary is 'highly favored'?

views.label: Fullness of grace, the source of grace
views.case: Jerome's Latin Vulgate rendered the word 'full of grace,' and the Catholic tradition has often understood it as a settled state of grace in Mary from the start, which is part of the basis for the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception. The perfect tense is taken to indicate a lasting condition.

views.label: One who has received favor
views.case: Protestants, and many scholars, hold that the verb means 'to show favor to,' and that the participle describes a person who has been the recipient of God's grace, not its source. Gabriel's next words, 'you have found favor with God,' verse 30, say the same thing in simple terms, and Mary herself says God is 'my Savior,' verse 47, which implies she too needs saving.

views.label: Both a gift and a calling
views.case: Others emphasize that the favour is tied to the task. She has been graced in order to bear the Son of the Most High, and Elizabeth's words, 'blessed are you among women,' verse 42, reflect the unique role, not a general state of holiness.

debates.bearing: Whatever one concludes about later doctrine, the text itself makes God the giver and Mary the recipient. The passage is about what God does through a humble servant, and it is she who points all the glory back to Him.

study.originalLanguages:
Gabriel's greeting in verse 28 contains the verb that stands behind the phrase 'highly favored,' kecharitomene, a perfect passive participle from the same family as charis, grace. The perfect tense marks a completed act with a lasting result, and the passive says God is the actor. The same verb appears in Ephesians 1:6, where God 'has freely given us' grace in the Beloved One. The word before it, chaire, is the ordinary Greek greeting, but the BSB footnote notes that it can also be rendered 'Rejoice.' Some readers hear in it an echo of Zephaniah 3:14-17, 'Sing for joy, O Daughter of Zion,' where the LORD is said to be in the midst of the city, which is close to Gabriel's next words, 'The Lord is with you.' The echo is a possibility, not a certainty.

The word 'virgin' in verse 27 is parthenos. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses to translate the Hebrew in Isaiah 7:14, where the Hebrew word almah can mean a young woman of marriageable age and the Greek translators chose parthenos. Matthew follows the Greek in quoting it, Matthew 1:23. In Luke the word is used twice in the one verse for Mary, and verse 34, 'I am a virgin,' makes the meaning of the word specific.

The name Jesus, Iesous, is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, 'the LORD saves.' Gabriel says 'you are to give Him the name Jesus,' verse 31, and Matthew spells out the meaning: 'He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21. The title in verse 32, 'Son of the Most High,' uses hypsistos, a name for God used in Genesis 14:18-22 and in Daniel, and it is the title used by demons in Luke 8:28, with a similar meaning.

In verse 35 'overshadow' is episkiazo. It is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses when the cloud 'settled' on the tent of meeting and the glory of the LORD filled it, Exodus 40:35, and Luke uses it again at the transfiguration, Luke 9:34. Gabriel uses the language of God's presence in a sanctuary to describe what happens in a young woman. The 'Holy One' is the One born to be called the Son of God, and Mary is a sanctuary in a sense that the language of the tabernacle suggests.

Verse 37, 'no word from God will ever fail,' is a verbal echo of the Greek of Genesis 18:14, where the Septuagint has 'Will a word be impossible with God?' The Greek word rhema, 'word, thing,' is what is in view. The BSB footnote gives an alternative, 'For nothing will be impossible with God.' Either way Gabriel's answer gathers up the story of Sarah.

The Magnificat's verbs are mostly in the aorist tense: He 'has done,' 'has scattered,' 'has brought down,' 'has filled.' Scholars debate whether the aorists describe what God has already done in Mary's case, in Israel's history, or in a confident anticipation of what He has started to do. Some call this a prophetic aorist, a way of speaking of a promised thing as already done. Luke's context supports reading it as both: God has begun the reversal in Mary, and she sings of its completion.

Finally, 'mercy,' eleos, in verses 50 and 54 stands behind the Old Testament word chesed, covenant love. Verse 54 puts it with the verb 'remembering,' mnesthenai, so that mercy and remembering belong together, as in Psalm 98:3, 'He has remembered His love and faithfulness to the house of Israel.' God's remembering is never only a mental act; it is the moment He acts for those He loves.

typology.type: Hannah, the song of the barren
typology.fulfillment: Hannah prayed for a son, was given Samuel, and sang that the LORD 'raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap,' 1 Samuel 2:8, and that 'the barren woman gives birth to seven,' 2:5. She ended by saying the LORD 'will give power to His king' and 'exalt the horn of His anointed,' 2:10, using the word anointed, the word from which 'messiah' comes. Mary's song takes Hannah's themes and carries them to their destination: the king whose horn is to be exalted is now conceived. The type falls short because Samuel anointed kings but Jesus is the King. Hannah gave her son to the sanctuary; Mary bears the one who is Himself the temple, John 2:19-21.

typology.type: The cloud that covered the tabernacle
typology.fulfillment: At the completion of the tabernacle 'the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle,' Exodus 40:34. Gabriel says that 'the power of the Most High will overshadow you,' verse 35, using the verb the Greek Old Testament uses for that cloud. John carries the thought on when he says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, using the language of tabernacling. The correspondence is that God comes to live among His people in a chosen place. The escalation is that the dwelling is now a person, and the place is a human womb. The type falls short because the tabernacle was a structure that could be moved and later destroyed; the Son is permanent.

typology.type: The throne of David and its son
typology.fulfillment: God promised David a son who would build a house for His name and whose kingdom would be established forever, 2 Samuel 7:12-13, and added, 'I will be his Father, and he will be My son,' 7:14. Solomon was the first fulfilment, but 7:14 also says 'when he does wrong, I will discipline him,' and Solomon did wrong. The line ended in exile. Gabriel's words, 'The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David,' verse 32, announce the son in whom the promise holds without failure. Peter says David knew God had sworn that one of his descendants would sit on his throne, and that the promise concerned the resurrection of the Christ, Acts 2:30-31. The type falls short in every earlier son: each died, and each stumbled.

typology.type: Isaac, the child of the promise
typology.fulfillment: Isaac was born to Abraham and Sarah when they were old, and God said 'you are to name him Isaac,' Genesis 17:19, as Gabriel says 'you are to give Him the name Jesus.' When Sarah doubted, the LORD asked, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' Genesis 18:14, which Gabriel recalls. Isaac's birth was a miracle of God's power in a body past age. Jesus' conception goes further, since it has no human father at all. Through Abraham's offspring all nations were to be blessed, Genesis 22:18, and Mary's closing line ties her child to that promise, verses 54 and 55. The type falls short because Isaac needed a substitute on the mountain, while Jesus is Himself the one provided.

study.christ:
This passage is the clearest statement of who Jesus is in all of Luke's opening chapters, and it is made by an angel before He is born. He is Jesus, 'the LORD saves,' a name given from heaven and not chosen by His parents, so the child's name is already His task. He is 'great,' and 'will be called the Son of the Most High,' verse 32. He is the heir of David, with 'the throne of His father David,' verse 32, and a reign over 'the house of Jacob forever,' verse 33. These are the promises of 2 Samuel 7 and Isaiah 9 compressed into two verses.

He is the Son of God by the Holy Spirit. The 'Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God,' verse 35. Paul gives the same two sides in Romans 1:3-4: a descendant of David 'according to the flesh' and 'declared with power to be the Son of God.' The conception does not make Him Son of God for the first time. It means the eternal Son takes human life. Paul says that 'God sent His Son, born of a woman,' Galatians 4:4, and John says that 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. Luke narrates the first step of that descent.

He is the seed of the woman. The promise of Genesis 3:15 was that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head, and the promise to Abraham was that through his offspring all nations would be blessed, Genesis 22:18. Mary sings in the last lines that God is 'remembering to be merciful, as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever,' verses 54 and 55. She is saying that the child in her womb is the end of the promise.

He is the one whose coming turns the world over. The reversals in the Magnificat are what Jesus will bring. He will say 'Blessed are you who are poor,' Luke 6:20, and read in Nazareth that He has come 'to preach good news to the poor,' Luke 4:18, and will eat with those the world looks down on. The most striking reversal is that the Lord of glory is born into poverty, and the Mighty One does His great things by taking the lowest place.

He is the one to whom Elizabeth gives the title 'my Lord,' verse 43, and at whose coming a child in the womb leaps with joy. Whatever the unborn John felt, Luke wants the reader to see that even before His birth the presence of Jesus brings joy and prophecy.

Mary herself needs the one she carries. 'My spirit rejoices in God my Savior,' verse 47, is said by a woman about to bear the Saviour. The relation of mother and child is, in another sense, that of the saved and her Saviour. This keeps the Gospel from becoming a story about Mary and returns it to what it is: a story about Jesus, and what He has come to do.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the one who initiates. Nothing in Mary's life led up to this, and she does not pray for it. 'God sent the angel Gabriel,' verse 26, and the favour comes before any merit. Mary says so in the song: 'the Mighty One has done great things for me,' verse 49. Salvation in Luke 1 is not something human beings achieve or earn but something God gives. The whole story depends on His decision.

He is the Most High, the Mighty One, the Holy One, and He draws near. The names used in this chapter stress His greatness: the Most High, verses 32 and 35, the Mighty One, verse 49, and 'Holy is His name,' verse 49. Yet He sends His angel to a village girl, comes to her by the Spirit, and is born as a child. Isaiah had said that the One who is high and lifted up dwells also 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit,' Isaiah 57:15. Mary's song is the praise of that God, and the Psalms say the same: 'Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly,' Psalm 138:6.

He is the God of the three persons in their work. In verse 35 the Holy Spirit comes on Mary, the power of the Most High overshadows her, and the child is called the Son of God. The Father, the Spirit and the Son are named together, long before the later church formulated the doctrine. The conception is the work of the whole God.

He is the God of mercy. Mary says His mercy 'extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation,' verse 50, which draws on Psalm 103:17. His mercy has a history and a future. It runs through the generations of the faithful, and it reaches the humble, not the proud. In the same song, He is the God who 'has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts,' verse 51. Mercy and justice sit together. He does not simply flatter the humble or crush the strong; He sets the world right, and the rule by which He does it is that He opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, as James and Peter later say, James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.

He is faithful to what He has promised. The final lines of the song speak of remembering, of mercy, and of Abraham. The God who made a promise to Abraham thousands of years earlier has not forgotten it. Gabriel says it as a principle, 'no word from God will ever fail,' verse 37, and Mary sings it as history.

He is a God who commands trust and gives signs. Gabriel gives Mary the sign of Elizabeth, verse 36, and she believes. God's way of calling people to faith includes, at times, a gracious sign, and not all requests for one are doubt.

For worship, the passage provides a pattern. Mary's soul magnifies the Lord. She does not make God larger, for He is already great, but she makes Him large in her sight, so that He fills the place of her fears. Her song begins with God, ends with God, and in between lists what He has done. Worship that follows her moves from what God has done for me to what He has done for the world, and rests in what He has promised.

crossReferences.note: Hannah's song is the great model of the Magnificat. She too rejoices in the LORD, says the mighty are broken and the feeble strengthened, the hungry fed, the poor raised from the dust, and ends with the LORD's king and anointed. Mary sings it again, now that the anointed is on His way.

God's promise to David of a descendant whose throne and kingdom would be established forever. Gabriel's words in verses 32 and 33 apply it to Jesus. It explains why the angel stresses 'the throne of His father David' and a kingdom that will never end.

'The virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.' Matthew 1:22-23 quotes it of Jesus' birth. Luke does not quote it but tells the story it describes, and the pairing of virgin, son and God with us runs through both accounts.

The Greek of Gabriel's words in verse 37 echoes the question put to Abraham about Sarah's old age: 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' The echo tells Mary, and the reader, that the conception will be another case of God doing what is beyond human strength.

The cloud covered the Tent of Meeting and 'the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.' Gabriel's verb for the Spirit 'overshadowing' Mary is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses of this cloud. Mary becomes the place where the glory of God dwells in a new way.

The LORD 'raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dump to seat them with nobles,' and 'settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother.' Both halves of the psalm lie behind the Magnificat and are fulfilled in Elizabeth and Mary at once.

'He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things.' Luke 1:53 uses almost the same words. The hungry of the Magnificat are the same people the psalm describes, those who cry to God and find that He is able to feed them.

'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?' and 'You will show faithfulness to Jacob and loving devotion to Abraham, as You swore to our fathers.' The closing lines of Mary's song, with mercy and Abraham together, echo the prophet's closing praise.

The prophet calls the Daughter of Zion to rejoice because 'the LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save.' Gabriel's 'Rejoice' and 'The Lord is with you' may echo this call, which would make Mary the person in whom the promised presence arrives.

The teaching of Jesus on the poor, the hungry and the rich turns the reversals of the Magnificat into blessings and woes. 'Blessed are you who are poor' and 'Woe to you who are rich' are the song of Mary spoken by her Son.

'When the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law.' Paul's whole account of the incarnation is a single sentence, and 'born of a woman' is what Luke 1:26-38 tells in detail. Mary is the woman and Gabriel's visit is the sending.

God 'chose the lowly and despised things of the world... so that no one may boast in His presence.' Paul says of the church what Mary says of herself: God's method is to take the humble and so to take away every ground for human pride.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story began with a promise made at the first loss. After Adam and Eve fell, God said that the woman's seed would crush the serpent, Genesis 3:15, and ever since then the story has followed that seed. It narrowed to Abraham, to whom God said all nations would be blessed through his offspring, Genesis 22:18, and to David, to whom He promised a son whose throne would last forever, 2 Samuel 7:13. Each promise was held in trust by a family, and each family kept failing. By Luke's day the line of David had no throne, Israel had no king of its own, and the promises seemed to have lapsed.

Luke 1:26-56 is where the line begins to arrive. Everything said to Abraham, to David and to Israel is named in this passage, and not one thing has been forgotten. The seed has been placed in the womb of a girl in a Galilean village, and the angel's words are a summary of the covenant promises. Mary, who has no standing and no power, is the means by which God does what He said He would do. That is the way He has worked since Abraham and Sarah: He starts again with what is humble, and does His great work through it.

Mary's song is a map of the whole Bible's moral shape. It sings creation's God, who is Mighty and Holy, the covenant God who remembers, and the redeemer who lifts the humble and brings down the proud. It is the gospel in miniature before the gospel has been told. The reversals in her song are carried out in the life of Jesus, who is born in a stable, dies a criminal's death and is raised, and in doing so overturns every human measure of power.

The story reaches forward from this point. The child will grow, announce the kingdom and die, and then rise, and the Spirit who overshadowed Mary will be poured out on the church in Acts. The promise of a kingdom without end waits for its completion, when the world is renewed. In the new creation, 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' and the One seated on the throne says, 'Behold, I make all things new,' Revelation 21:4-5. The throne of David and the throne of God are the same throne, and the child announced to a village girl is the king who sits on it.

Mary's last word in the passage is not about herself. It is that God has helped His servant Israel, 'remembering to be merciful, as He promised.' The story ends where it began, with a faithful God who keeps what He has said.

sermon.title: Mary's Song
sermon.why: Keller expounds Luke 1:39-55, Mary's Magnificat, tracing what leads her to sing and the God she sings about, the Savior who regards the lowly and overturns human pride. A rich, Christ-centered handling of the Magnificat at the heart of this movement.

quiz.q: What did Gabriel tell Mary about the child she would bear?

options.text: He would be the Son of the Most High and would reign on David's throne forever.
options.note: Verses 32 and 33 give the child's divine identity and everlasting kingship.

options.text: He would be a great prophet like Elijah.
options.note: That description fits John, not Jesus; Jesus is the Son of the Most High and King.

options.text: He would be named Jesus and bring her joy.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits the heart of the promise, His divine sonship and reign.

options.text: He would be a wealthy ruler in Rome.
options.note: His throne is David's, and His kingdom is not of earthly wealth or Rome.

quiz.q: How would Mary conceive this child?

options.text: The Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her.
options.note: Verse 35 gives the miraculous conception by the Holy Spirit.

options.text: God would work a miracle so that the child would be holy, the Son of God.
options.note: True and stated, but it does not name the specific means, the Holy Spirit's work.

options.text: In the ordinary way, once she and Joseph were married.
options.note: Mary was a virgin; the conception was by the Spirit, not ordinary means.

options.text: Through the priesthood in the temple.
options.note: The conception had nothing to do with the temple; it was the Spirit's miracle.

quiz.q: How did Mary respond to Gabriel's announcement?

options.text: She humbly submitted, saying, I am the Lord's servant; may it happen according to your word.
options.note: Verse 38 records her trusting surrender.

options.text: She asked how it could be, since she was a virgin.
options.note: She did ask this, but her question led to faith and surrender, unlike Zechariah's doubt.

options.text: She demanded a sign before she would believe.
options.note: That was closer to Zechariah's response; Mary trusted the word.

options.text: She refused the calling out of fear.
options.note: She did not refuse; she gladly offered herself as the Lord's servant.

quiz.q: What is the central theme of Mary's Magnificat?

options.text: God is a mighty and merciful Savior who lifts up the lowly and casts down the proud.
options.note: The song's great theme is God's saving reversal, verses 46 to 55.

options.text: God has done great things for Mary personally.
options.note: True and part of the song, but it widens to God's dealings with all the humble and with Israel.

options.text: Mary is worthy of praise for her own goodness.
options.note: Mary magnifies the Lord and calls Him her Savior; the praise is His, not hers.

options.text: God rewards the rich and powerful above all.
options.note: The song says the opposite: He sends the rich away empty and fills the hungry.

quiz.q: Whom did Mary say her spirit rejoiced in?

options.text: God her Savior.
options.note: Verse 47 names God as her Savior, showing she too needed saving grace.

options.text: The Mighty One who had done great things for her.
options.note: True and closely related, but the exact phrase is God my Savior.

options.text: The child she would bear.
options.note: Her joy centers on God the Savior, though it is bound up with the child He gives.

options.text: Herself, for being chosen.
options.note: Her rejoicing is in God, not in herself.

questions: Gabriel greeted Mary as one who had found favor with God, sheer grace rather than reward. Where do you need to rest in God's free favor rather than trying to earn His acceptance?
Mary answered, I am the Lord's servant. Is there a place where God is calling you to a costly yes, and what makes it hard to surrender as she did?
Elizabeth's baby leaped for joy at the nearness of Christ. What stirs joy in you when you draw near to Jesus, and how might you seek more of that gladness?
The Magnificat celebrates a God who lifts the lowly and humbles the proud. How does that reversal challenge the way you measure success and worth?
Mary rejoiced in God her Savior, counting herself among those in need of saving. How does knowing your own need of grace shape your worship?

translationNotes.note: Highly favored translates a word meaning one who has been shown grace; the BSB footnote notes that the greeting can be rendered Rejoice, and that some manuscripts add Blessed are you among women, words that appear again in Elizabeth's greeting in verse 42.
For no word from God will ever fail is rendered in a footnote as For nothing will be impossible with God; both capture the promise that God's spoken word carries its own power to come true.
My soul magnifies the Lord translates the verb that gives the song its traditional name, the Magnificat, from the Latin. To magnify is to declare and delight in God's greatness, not to add to it.
